Price caps are our calculation from the measure (125% of the county conforming loan limit in the FHFA's annual report). Forty-one counties sit at the 2026 baseline limit of $832,750, so their cap is $1,040,938; ten Bay Area and Southern California counties sit at the $1,249,125 ceiling, so their cap is $1,561,406. Income ceilings use HCD's 2026 State Income Limits as an illustration; the measure says CalHFA will apply "the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area," adjusted for family size, and the agency has not yet said which income table it would use.
PPIC's Eric McGhee calculated (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/) in October that 91% of California renters would have met the income test in 2024, the most recent Census year, and that the price cap "would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024," about 50% above that December's statewide median. Eligibility, he wrote, "is not purchasing power": at 7% mortgage rates and Fannie Mae's 36% debt-to-income ceiling, an entry-level new home was out of reach for 56% of renters even with the down payment solved.
California's existing down payment programs defer repayment while Prop 37's loan is repaid monthly:
CalHFA already runs down payment help, and the comparison explains most of the debate. Its MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) is a "deferred-payment junior loan" of up to 3.5% of the price on an FHA loan or 3% on a conventional one, for first-time buyers within CalHFA's income limits, with nothing due until the home is sold, refinanced or paid off. Its Dream For All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/index.htm) lends up to 20% of the price, capped at $150,000, to first-generation and first-time buyers, and is repaid with the original amount plus 20% of the home's appreciation (15% for buyers at or below 80% of area median income) when the home changes hands. Dream For All is funded by budget appropriations and rationed by lottery; the 2026 application portal closed on March 16 and vouchers went out in May. Proposition 1 on the same ballot would add $1.1 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) in general obligation bond money for homeownership programs of this deferred kind, aimed at low- and moderate-income first-time buyers.
Prop 37's loan is different in three ways. It is open to anyone under 200% of AMI, not only first-time buyers. It is repaid monthly, because the bonds behind it have to be serviced from borrowers' payments. And it is limited to new construction. The California Budget & Policy Center's analysis (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/) puts the first two together: the silent-second structure of today's programs "ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn't compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family's monthly budget," while Prop 37's second mortgage "could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates," because investors in bonds backed by second liens "may therefore require a higher return." The measure's hardship clause lets a borrower ask CalHFA to defer "monthly interest payments" temporarily, which the Budget Center reads as confirmation that monthly payments are the design.

The proponents' case for monthly repayment is the cost it replaces. Buyers who put down less than 20% usually pay private mortgage insurance until they build equity, and the McClatchy editorial board, which recommends (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317470188.html) a yes vote, wrote that proponents "have modeled relatively high second-mortgage rates and found buyers could still save money compared with private mortgage insurance." Nothing in the text guarantees a below-market rate; the argument in favor promises "below-market, fixed-rate loans," and the Orange County Register's editorial board wrote (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/20/endorsement-no-on-proposition-37-a-risky-25-billion-housing-experiment/) that the claim "rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%," failing which CalHFA "will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates."
Prop 37's qualified builder option trades labor standards for modified construction-defect rules:
Any developer can sell homes into the program. Section 51515.02 adds a voluntary "qualified builder option" for those who certify to CalHFA that their homes will meet the program's eligibility rules; the agency must confirm participation within 30 days, and the letter can be used to market and finance the project. A participating builder takes on the labor and enforcement provisions of Public Resources Code section 21080.66 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21080.66), the 2025 infill-housing CEQA exemption, which require prevailing wages on fully affordable projects, apply the state's skilled-workforce standards to buildings over 85 feet, extend wage-theft liability under Labor Code section 218.8 to the developer, and let joint labor-management committees sue contractors on workers' behalf. The builder also becomes liable for its contractors' and subcontractors' unemployment-insurance, workers' compensation and licensing violations.
In exchange, homes built under the option get a modified version of the Right to Repair Act's pre-litigation process. A defect notice must identify each home and each alleged violation and be signed by each homeowner; the builder may communicate directly with homeowners during the process; the builder may obtain a written release for completed repairs, which current law, as the LAO's letter notes, does not allow; a builder may move to dismiss a stayed case if the homeowner has not acted within 120 days; and the builder must disclose the special rules in writing before escrow closes. For any qualified new home, built under the option or not, attorneys' contingency fees in a defect case are capped at 30% of the recovery unless a court approves more. The modified procedures fall away if a builder sells a home for more than 25% above the price cap, a point proponent Robert Hertzberg confirmed to the Register's board. The California Conference of Carpenters is a signer of the ballot argument and its affiliates have given $1.7 million to the campaign.
Proposition 37's second mortgages are exempt from a 2025 foreclosure-protection law and carry a 0.5% fee cap:
Section 51515.04 sets the consumer rules. CalHFA must limit lender fees, ban prepayment penalties and require fixed rates. A lender may charge an origination fee of no more than 0.5% or $290, whichever is greater, and no other fee without the agency's approval. An applicant whose credit score falls short may submit bank statements, pay stubs and rent history for "cashflow underwriting." Every applicant must retain a licensed California real estate agent or broker "to ensure that the home buyer receives adequate representation." CalHFA must require homeowner education where it would help and provide for an independent annual audit.
One clause runs the other way. Subdivision (g) states that Civil Code section 2924.13 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2924.13) "shall not apply to any middle-class home ownership loans made under this chapter." That section, added by AB 130 in June 2025, targets dormant second mortgages: it makes it an unlawful practice for a subordinate-mortgage servicer to go three years without writing to the borrower, to skip required transfer notices, or to foreclose on a debt it has reported as written off or after the statute of limitations has run, and it requires a recorded certification of compliance before any nonjudicial foreclosure. Prop 37 loans, which are subordinate mortgages serviced by CalHFA's contracted lenders, would sit outside those rules. The text does not say why.
The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state cost and three unknowns for Proposition 37:
The LAO's ballot analysis and its October 6, 2025 letter reach the same conclusion in nearly the same words: because the measure "uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs." The letter adds that the $25 billion "is in addition to the revenue bonds CalHFA already issues" for its other programs. Both documents then list what cannot be known yet: "the extent to which investors want to buy the bond," "how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options," and "whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying."
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) does not count Prop 37 at all. It lists two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, Propositions 1 and 38, at about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. The closest precedent for a self-repaying housing bond is in Prop 1 itself: its $1.25 billion veterans' home-loan bond is repaid by borrowers, and the LAO notes those payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds." The difference is that veterans' bonds are general obligation bonds the state stands behind if payments fall short; Prop 37's are revenue bonds that, by their own terms, it does not. The McClatchy board raised the political version of that risk: borrowers in trouble "will quickly discover that their second mortgage exists because California created and authorized this program," which "could create an expectation that the state bears some responsibility for protecting them."
Proposition 37's reach depends on interest rates and new construction, according to PPIC and the Budget Center:
The campaign says the measure "is expected to spur construction of roughly 190,000 new homes." California YIMBY, which took no position (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-37-2026/), worked the arithmetic the other way: $25 billion over 190,000 homes is about $130,000 of bond money per home, and the group argued "there is no shortage of buyers" for new ownership housing, so the subsidy would mostly raise prices unless it reached weaker markets. PPIC's McGhee estimated that if every loan went to a home at the maximum price with the full 17%, $25 billion would reach about 113,000 buyers; at the full 17% on entry-level homes, about 560,000, which he called "a reasonable central estimate." California would have needed 1.35 million more owner households in 2024 to match the rest of the country, and the 560,000 figure would close about 41% of that gap.
The homeownership gap is the proponents' starting point. The Census Bureau's state table (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates/tab3_state05_2026_hmr.xlsx) puts California's homeownership rate at 54.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest of the 50 states except New York (52.4%), against a national rate (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/files/qtr226/Q226press.pdf) of 65.0%. The argument in favor says a 20% down payment on a median home "can require saving over $186,000"; the California Association of Realtors' latest report (https://www.car.org/en/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/august2026sales) put the median existing single-family price at $901,420 in August 2026, which makes 20% about $180,000 and 3% about $27,000. The Budget Center notes that the median California household held "just over $18,000" in checking and savings in 2025, so even 3% "could still almost or entirely clear out" what a typical family has, and that new homes more often carry HOA dues, Mello-Roos assessments and insurance problems in fire-prone areas.
Proposition 37's Yes side reports $30.9 million from Realtors, carpenters and Building a Better California with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $30.9 million in support of Prop 37 across two committees and no opposition committee large enough to appear. The main committee, "Yes on 37—California Homeownership," lists $23.9 million from its top contributors: $14.85 million from Homeownership for Families, a committee sponsored by the California Association of Realtors whose own top donors are the Realtors' Issues Mobilization PAC and the National Association of Realtors; $6 million from Building a Better California, the committee funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr that is also the main opponent of the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/); $1.25 million from the National Association of Realtors; $1.7 million from three carpenters' union committees; $50,000 from California Forever, the Solano County new-town developer; and $30,358 from the California Democratic Party. The Realtors' Homeownership for Families committee is listed separately with $7 million from the Realtors' PAC and the national association.
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-37-creates-loan-program-middle-income-buyers-qualified-new-homes-initiative-statute), which runs through October 6, shows $19.6 million for the Yes committee and "No committees identified" in opposition; the FPPC's later date accounts for the gap. The petition that qualified the measure was paid for by "CA Homes Committee," with major funding from Building a Better California, the California Association of Realtors and the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, according to the Secretary of State's Official Top Funders (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/1990-top-funders-02-02-26.pdf) filing. The Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) lists Robert M. Hertzberg, the former Assembly Speaker and Senate majority leader, as proponent on A.G. File 25-0013A1, titled October 21, 2025. The Budget Center observes that because revenue bonds need no voter approval, the program "could have been enacted legislatively."
The argument for Proposition 37 promises zero taxpayer cost and no argument against was filed:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Danny Curtin of the California Conference of Carpenters, Treasurer Fiona Ma as a CalHFA board member and David West of the California State Commanders Veterans Council, says the measure "creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction—with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS." It says California "has the second-worst homeownership rate in 

[Showing characters 20000 to 40000 of 68147. Call web_fetch with offset 40000 to keep reading.]

the nation," that "a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000," and that the program "is not a handout" because borrowers "must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans." It quotes Controller Malia Cohen: "downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers." The guide's index lists the United Nurses Associations of California, the California Conference of Carpenters and Ma as supporters.
The page for the argument against reads: "NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED." CalMatters' voter guide lists Reform California and the League of Women Voters of California as opponents, summarizing their case as objections to the state entering the mortgage business and to helping buyers only by adding debt. The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 37 leads 61% to 35% with Newsom, Becerra and Democrats in support and editorial boards split:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 61% yes, 35% no and 3% undecided, the strongest support for any of the 14 measures. Democrats back it 76% to 20% and independents 62% to 35%, while Republicans oppose it 62% to 35%. Renters support it 70% to 28% and homeowners 59% to 38%; voters under 35 back it 69% to 26% and those 55 and older 54% to 42%. Five percent named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's September poll did not ask about it, and PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom endorsed the measure on October 9, saying (https://voteyeson37.com/press-release-governor-newsom-supports-prop-37-to-expand-homeownership-in-california/) in the campaign's release that it is "a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families—at zero cost or risk to taxpayers." Xavier Becerra listed (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/?p=551) it among his yes votes on July 31. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) is neutral, one of two measures on which it takes no side; the other is Proposition 1. The campaign's site lists Controller Cohen, Treasurer Ma, Superintendent Tony Thurmond, San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan, Darrell Steinberg, Antonio Villaraigosa, Katie Porter and SEIU among its endorsers.
Editorial boards divided on the second-mortgage question. McClatchy's California papers recommend yes, with stated reservations, on the ground that low-down buyers already pay for private mortgage insurance and that the program "connects assistance to new housing," while asking CalHFA to build a public dashboard of rates, defaults and foreclosures. The San Francisco Chronicle recommends a yes vote, according to CalMatters' roster of editorials. The San Diego Union-Tribune (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/) recommends no, writing that the measure "doesn't do in the slightest" anything about "shelter's extreme cost," and the Orange County Register recommends no, calling it "a risky $25 billion housing experiment" that leaves income-limited families with "two mortgage payments."
Proposition 37 after November 3 would give CalHFA a year to launch the middle-class homeownership loan:
If Prop 37 passes, it takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State certifies the results, which is due December 11, and CalHFA would have until late 2027 to adopt its rules, sign up lenders and begin selling bonds. The agency would then set the interest rate, the credit standards and the pace of bond sales, which is where the measure's unknowns get answered: whether investors buy second-lien revenue bonds at a rate that undercuts private mortgage insurance, whether builders enroll in the qualified builder option, and whether buyers who can clear 3% and a first mortgage at current rates appear in the numbers the campaign projects. The Legislature could amend the statute only by a 60% vote of each house and only in ways that "further the purposes" of the act. If it fails, CalHFA keeps running MyHome and Dream For All, and the only new homeownership money on this ballot is Proposition 1's $1.1 billion for its deferred-loan programs.
This article reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FHFA's 2026 conforming loan limits and HCD's 2026 income limits, campaign-finance data as of October 14, 2026 (FPPC) and October 6, 2026 (Secretary of State), party and gubernatorial positions as of October 18, 2026, and polling fielded September 4–10, 2026.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.
California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.

Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.
